author: William Saville

title: Rain in the Second Kitchen
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass three
content:
The roof began leaking just as Iroh declared that the evening would be peaceful.

A drop of water landed in his tea.

He stared at the surface.

Another drop followed.

"Ah," he said.

I looked up.

The ceiling above the front counter had developed a dark seam. Rainwater ran along it, gathered at the lowest point, and fell directly into the pot of jasmine leaves.

"Please tell me that's a new blend," I said.

"Only if we intend to serve roof."

By the time we moved the tea, three customers were holding cups in their laps to protect them from the ceiling. Iroh apologized, offered fresh drinks from the back, and asked them to use the side entrance until the leak could be inspected.

Mara appeared at the door with a basket of bread and took in the scene.

"Oh, lovely," she said. "Indoor weather."

"An exciting new service," Iroh replied.

"Charge extra."

We moved the tables away from the wet floor. The shop wasn't flooded, but the water had found a narrow channel down the wall, and the front room smelled of damp plaster. The roof had been patched after the last storm. Apparently someone had missed a seam.

Tamsin arrived with a ladder and an expression that suggested she was tired of buildings having opinions.

"I can't climb onto wet slate," she told us. "Not safely. I'll seal the interior drip and inspect the roof when it dries."

Iroh nodded.

"Then we shall close early."

"Good."

She looked surprised by how quickly he agreed.

He noticed.

"I have learned that hospitality does not require guests to swim."

That left the two of us, a mountain of cups, and the second kitchen.

It was barely large enough for a person to turn around without becoming intimately acquainted with a shelf. The old stove sat against one wall. A narrow table occupied the other, and a basket of spare cloths lived beneath it.

I carried in a kettle. Iroh carried the tea tins.

We collided in the doorway.

"After you," he said.

"There's nowhere for me to go."

"Then perhaps we should invent a new direction."

I stepped sideways. He stepped the same way. The kettle knocked against the door frame.

We both laughed.

The back kitchen had always been our quiet place, but quiet looked different when two people were trying to run a business from it. The shelf smelled of ginger and dried citrus. A tiny window faced the garden, where the rain had turned the path into a series of bright dark stones.

I put the dirty cups in the washbasin.

Iroh reached for the clean ones.

We bumped elbows.

"You're doing that on purpose," I said.

"Would it improve your opinion of me if I were?"

"Probably not."

"Then I shall maintain my innocence."

By the third collision, I was warm enough to suspect he had turned the kitchen into a game. He was smiling too much for a man whose roof had leaked into his tea.

We worked until the last cup was clean. Then we took inventory. The damaged tea had to be discarded. Two tins of the expensive blend had survived. One crate of cups would need washing again when the dust settled.

The numbers added up to a loss we couldn't ignore.

Iroh studied the page.

"We can afford the roof repair," he said. "But the next order of mountain mint will be smaller."

I leaned against the counter.

"You hate reducing the good tea."

"I hate choosing which good thing to give up."

"Then we choose carefully."

He looked at me, tired but amused.

"You sound like Neri."

"That's insulting."

"Only a little."

We made a temporary menu for the back kitchen, four drinks instead of twelve. A sign at the front door explained the closure, the rain damage, and when customers could expect an update. No promise of tomorrow. No claim that the weather owed us cooperation.

By evening the storm had begun to ease.

Mina arrived with a damp inventory sheet and a sharper expression than the weather deserved.

"The roof isn't the only problem," she said. "Two of the clean tea tins were under the leak. They're closed, but I don't know whether the water got inside."

Iroh reached for one. Mina stopped him.

"We don't use it until we've checked it properly. I can mark it as held stock."

"Of course," he said.

She handed him the chalk. He wrote HOLD — INSPECTION beside the tins, then looked almost offended that such a small word could keep him from serving tea.

We moved the containers to a dry shelf and recorded how much stock was still safe. The repair estimate would have to include the damaged plaster and the work needed to check for lingering dampness, not just a patch where the water had fallen. Tamsin had already told us that a dry afternoon wasn't proof the structure could take another storm.

"Will the customers be disappointed?" I asked.

"Certainly," Iroh said. "They may choose the smaller menu, or return when we can offer more."

He sounded sad. I touched his sleeve.

"You've built a place people like," I said. "They can keep liking it while a room is closed."

He looked toward the front counter. "I wonder why I find that difficult to believe."

"Because you're terrible at letting anything unfinished stay unfinished."

"An accusation made with troubling confidence."

I smiled. Mina had gone home at her agreed hour. We were alone with the rain, the little candle and a kitchen that smelled of wet plaster.

"Do you want to sit with me for a while?" I asked.

"Very much."

He took my hand before we went to the table. There was no need to make the leak romantic, and no reason affection had to wait until every repair was finished.

Iroh lit one candle on the narrow table. I stood beside the stove, rolling my shoulders to loosen the ache from moving furniture.

"Come here," he said.

"What for?"

"Your shoulders."

"I can still move them."

"An achievement. Come here anyway."

I went.

He placed his hands on either side of my neck and began working his thumbs into the tense muscles beneath my collar. He was careful, pausing whenever I shifted. The warmth of his hands moved slowly through the ache.

"Better?" he asked.

"Much."

"Then perhaps you will stop trying to carry the whole teahouse by yourself."

"That sounds suspiciously like advice you should take."

"Many of my finest teachings are things I have difficulty practicing."

I turned toward him. Our faces were close. The candlelight softened the lines beside his eyes, and the faint smell of jasmine clung to his sleeve.

"You don't have to pretend the leak doesn't bother you," I said.

"I know."

"Does it?"

"Very much."

I smiled.

He laughed quietly.

"I am fond of this shop," he admitted. "I built parts of it with my hands. I like knowing that people can come here and feel safe, even for the length of a cup of tea. When the roof leaks, it feels like I have failed to protect that promise."

"A roof is allowed to fail without making its owner a failure."

"An irritatingly sensible observation."

"Learned from somebody."

He rested his forehead lightly against mine.

"Who could that be?"

"I believe he has a very fine beard."

"An excellent teacher, then."

I kissed him. He answered with the patient warmth I knew so well, then drew me closer when I slipped my hands around his waist. The little kitchen felt suddenly smaller, though I didn't mind.

He smiled against my mouth.

"The kettle is behind you."

"I know."

"And the table is behind me."

"I know."

"We have very little room."

"Then perhaps," I whispered, "we should stop trying to move."

He laughed, soft and delighted. We stood together until the candle burned low and the rain became a whisper against the window.

When we finally locked the shop, he asked whether I wanted to stay the night.

"Yes," I said.

We went upstairs, leaving the clean cups drying in the second kitchen. The rest of the evening needed no audience.

In the morning, the ceiling still had a stain. Tamsin returned with safe weather and a repair estimate. We signed the work order, posted the limited menu, and began again.

Iroh poured the first fresh cup for himself.

He examined it carefully.

"No roof," I said.

"A pity. I had considered patenting the blend."

I laughed, and he handed the second cup to me.
